A reference-counting garbage collector may leak memory because it depends solely on reference counts to determine if an object can be reclaimed. If there are reference cycles, where two or more objects reference each other but are otherwise unreachable from the program's root, their reference counts will never reach zero, and thus, they won't be collected, resulting in a memory leak.

In contrast, a stop-and-copy garbage collector does not rely on reference counts. Instead, it traces all reachable objects starting from the root set and copies them to a new memory region. Unreachable objects, including those in reference cycles, are not copied and are collected. Therefore, a stop-and-copy garbage collector can properly collect memory that a reference-counting collector would leak.

Instead of ensuring immediate update visibility, NFS provides close-to-open consistency semantics. This means that any updates made to a file by program A are guaranteed to be visible to program B only after the file is closed by A and subsequently opened by B. This model balances performance and consistency by minimizing network overhead while ensuring that changes are eventually visible.
